answers.question: Is shade-grown coffee under trees counted as forest?
answers.answer:
Generally, no. Under the EUDR definition, an “agricultural plantation” includes agroforestry systems where crops are grown under tree cover, and agricultural plantations of relevant commodities other than wood are excluded from “forest.” [EUDR Art. 2(6)] The recital likewise states that agroforestry systems—including crops grown under tree cover—“should not be considered forests,” but agricultural use [EUDR Recital 37].

Thus, shade-grown coffee under trees would generally be treated as agricultural use rather than forest, insofar as it falls within such an agroforestry or agricultural-plantation system. The passages do not resolve every factual classification, such as whether the land is actually used for coffee production or whether other characteristics place it outside that category. Map overlap alone does not establish that it is forest or non-compliant [Note: JRC GFC2020 forest map and coffee].

answers.question: What is the legal definition of forest?
answers.answer: Under the EUDR, “forest” means land spanning more than 0.5 hectares with trees higher than 5 metres and canopy cover exceeding 10%, or trees capable of reaching those thresholds in situ, excluding land predominantly under agricultural or urban use [EUDR Art. 2(4)]. Agricultural plantations—including fruit, oil-palm and olive plantations and agroforestry systems—are expressly excluded [EUDR Art. 2(6)]. Commission guidance indicates that urban use is predominant, for example, in parks and gardens in urban areas, regardless of whether the thresholds are met [EC Guidance §11.3 (part 2)]. The definition can include qualifying mangroves, forest roads and firebreaks, and qualifying areas outside legally designated forest land [EC Guidance §11.3 (part 2)]. It leaves open the treatment of “other wooded land” and other ecosystems beyond forests, which the Commission is to assess under the review procedure [EC FAQ Q4.13].

answers.question: What does deforestation mean in this regulation?
answers.answer:
Under the Regulation, “deforestation” means “the conversion of forest to agricultural use,” whether caused by humans or not [EUDR Art. 2(3)]. This includes a natural disaster where, for example, a forest fire is followed by conversion of the affected forest into agricultural land after the relevant cut-off date [EC FAQ Q4.12]. If the forest is allowed to regenerate, that situation is not considered deforestation [EC FAQ Q4.12].

Conversion of forest to other uses—such as urban development or infrastructure—does not fall within this definition [EC FAQ Q4.11]. The definition therefore leaves open questions outside conversion to agricultural use, including how particular land-use changes should be classified.

answers.question: What is the cut-off date for deforestation-free products?
answers.answer: The cut-off date is 31 December 2020. Under the EUDR definition, relevant commodities must have been produced on land not subject to deforestation after 31 December 2020; for wood products, the wood must also have been harvested without inducing forest degradation after that date [EUDR Art. 2(13)]. The Commission describes compliance checks as looking backwards to determine whether cropland was previously forest since 31 December 2020 [EC FAQ Q5.12]. The recital explains that this date was selected to prevent deforestation and forest degradation during the Regulation’s negotiation period [EUDR Recital 46].

answers.question: What is forest degradation?
answers.answer:
“Forest degradation” means structural changes to forest cover involving the conversion of:  

- primary forests or naturally regenerating forests into plantation forests or other wooded land; or  
- primary forests into planted forests [EUDR Art. 2(7)].

The definition therefore concerns transformation between specified forest types, not harvesting levels alone. Different harvesting levels are allowed where they do not cause such a transformation [EC FAQ Q4.4]. Operators should assess the forest type before and through 31 December 2020 and whether harvesting or planned post-harvesting activities cause or induce conversion to another forest type covered by the definition [EC FAQ Q4.6 (part 1)].

Planting or seeding for protection or ecosystem restoration, or forests that at maturity resemble naturally regenerating forests, may fall within the relevant exclusions and therefore not constitute degradation [EC FAQ Q4.9].

answers.question: When is a polygon needed for the geolocation of a plot?
answers.answer:
A polygon is needed when the plot is more than four hectares and is used to produce a relevant commodity other than cattle. The geolocation must then use “sufficient latitude and longitude points to describe the perimeter” of that plot [EUDR Art. 2(28)]. Commission guidance confirms that polygons—not a central point with a circumference—must be used in this situation [EC FAQ Q1.16].

Each polygon should describe one single plot of land. If a product contains commodities from several plots, several polygons must be included in the due diligence statement [EC FAQ Q1.14]. The passages do not specify a different polygon threshold or method for cattle plots; they also note that the threshold may be reviewed in the future [EUDR Art. 34(2)].

answers.question: From what date does the EUDR apply?
answers.answer:
The EUDR entered into force on 29 June 2023, but its substantive provisions generally apply from 30 December 2026 [EC FAQ Q8.1]. The specified obligations, including Articles 3–13, 16–24, 26, 31 and 32, apply from that date [EUDR Art. 38(2)].

For operators established as micro-undertakings or small undertakings by 31 December 2024, those provisions generally apply from 30 June 2027, subject to special rules for products covered by the EU Timber Regulation [EC Guidance §3 (part 1)] [EC FAQ Q8.1]. The transitional period runs from 29 June 2023 until the day before the applicable entry-into-application date [EC FAQ Q9.5].

answers.question: When does the regulation apply to micro and small undertakings?
answers.answer:
For micro- and small undertakings established as such by 31 December 2024, the EUDR’s relevant provisions generally apply from 30 June 2027, rather than 30 December 2026 [EUDR Art. 38(3)] [EC FAQ Q8.1]. This covers operators irrespective of their legal form and includes the obligations in Articles 3–13, 16–24, 26, 31 and 32 [EC Guidance §3 (part 1)]. The deferral does not apply to products covered by the Annex to Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 (the EUTR) [EUDR Art. 38(3)] [EC Guidance §3 (part 1)].

Whether an undertaking qualifies is determined under Article 3(1) or Article 3(2), first subparagraph, of Directive 2013/34/EU, using the thresholds in force on 31 December 2024 [EUDR Art. 38(3)] [EC FAQ Q3.10]. The passages do not specify those micro- and small-undertaking thresholds.

answers.question: What information and geolocation must operators collect?
answers.answer:
Operators must collect, organise and retain for five years information and evidence for each relevant product, including: a product description (including trade name, type, and, for wood, species’ common and full scientific names, plus contained or used commodities); quantity; country of production and relevant parts; and the production date or time range [EUDR Art. 9(1)]. They must collect the geolocation of all plots of land where the relevant commodities were produced; products sourced from different plots require the geolocation of those plots [EUDR Art. 9(1)].  

For micro or small primary operators, this geolocation may be replaced by the postal address of all plots or the establishment from which the commodities were produced [EUDR Art. 4a(5)]. Operators must verify and be able to prove that the geolocation or permitted postal address is correct [EC FAQ Q1.12]. National prohibitions on sharing data do not remove the collection and submission obligation [EC FAQ Q1.31].

answers.question: Can competent authorities use satellite imagery in their checks?
answers.answer: Yes. Competent authorities may use satellite imagery as part of their checks. The EUDR expressly permits “technical and scientific means” to determine whether products are deforestation-free, including Earth observation data from Copernicus and other publicly or privately available relevant sources [EUDR Art. 18(2)]. The Commission states that spatial imagery tools can help competent authorities perform checks, but the Regulation does not require any specific satellite tool or minimum resolution [EC FAQ Q5.18]. Authorities may use global, regional, national maps, or other appropriate sources; however, the Global Forest Cover 2020 map is not intended to be a definitive compliance source [EC FAQ Q9.10.1 (part 2)].

answers.question: Is coffee one of the relevant commodities?
answers.answer: Yes. Coffee is expressly listed as a “relevant commodity” under the EUDR definition [EUDR Art. 2(1)]. The Regulation also identifies coffee among the commodities covered where relevant products contain, have been fed with, or have been made using them [EUDR Art. 1(1)]. The recital likewise refers to coffee as one of the commodities whose Union consumption and production may contribute to deforestation [EUDR Recital 8]. The passages do not specify which coffee products are “relevant products”; that depends on the products listed in Annex I [EUDR Art. 1(1)].

answers.question: Does tree loss in the Hansen dataset prove deforestation?
answers.answer: No. Hansen tree-cover loss does not, by itself, prove EUDR deforestation. Under Article 2(3), deforestation requires “conversion of forest to agricultural use,” whether human-induced or not [EUDR Art. 2(3)]. Commission guidance says the relevant question is whether forest was converted to agricultural use, and that conversion to other non-agricultural land uses is not deforestation [EC Guidance §11.2 (part 1)]. The Hansen dataset records loss of tree canopy, which may result from clearing, pruning, storms, fire, or plantation harvest, and does not establish conversion to agricultural use [Note: Hansen Global Forest Change loss is not deforestation]. Therefore, Hansen loss may be evidence of tree-cover loss, but additional evidence is needed to determine whether the land was forest and was converted to agricultural use. The dataset alone leaves those elements open [EUDR Art. 2(3)][Note: Hansen Global Forest Change loss is not deforestation].

answers.question: Does the EUDR agricultural-use exclusion mean coffee cultivated under shade trees is not forest?
answers.answer: Generally, no. The EUDR expressly defines an “agricultural plantation” to include agroforestry systems “where crops are grown under tree cover,” and excludes agricultural plantations from “forest” [EUDR Art. 2(6)]. The recital likewise says agroforestry systems, including crops grown under tree cover, should not be considered forests but constitute agricultural use [EUDR Recital 37]. Thus, coffee cultivated under shade trees would generally fall outside the forest definition where it is an agroforestry or other agricultural production system. However, the passages do not establish that every coffee plot with trees automatically qualifies: the forest definition also turns on the land’s predominant use, while the agricultural-plantation definition concerns tree stands in agricultural production systems [EUDR Art. 2(4)].

answers.question: Under the EUDR, can land recorded as coffee under shade trees since 1998 still be forest when forest maps show tree cover?
answers.answer: Yes. Land recorded as coffee since 1998 can still qualify as “forest” if it exceeds 0.5 hectares, has trees over 5 metres (or able to reach that height), canopy cover above 10%, and is not predominantly under agricultural or urban land use [EUDR Art. 2(4)]. The definition must be assessed by those characteristics simultaneously [EC Guidance §11.3 (part 1)]. However, the passages do not establish whether the coffee use is “predominantly” agricultural land use in the particular case, so the 1998 record alone does not resolve the issue [EUDR Art. 2(4)][EC Guidance §11.3 (part 1)]. A forest-map indication is not conclusive: GFC 2020 is only one possible source, and coffee plantations are excluded from that map’s forest classification [EC FAQ Q9.10.1 (part 1)].

answers.question: Does tree-cover loss within an existing coffee plantation constitute deforestation under the EUDR?
answers.answer:
Tree-cover loss within an existing coffee plantation is not, by itself, “deforestation” under the EUDR. Deforestation requires “the conversion of forest to agricultural use” [EC Guidance §11.1 (part 1)]. Coffee plantations are agricultural plantations, and “all plantations of relevant commodities other than wood” are excluded from the EUDR definition of forest [EUDR Art. 2(6)]; the Commission likewise states that coffee plantations are excluded from forest [EC FAQ Q9.10.1 (part 1)].

Therefore, loss of canopy within land already classified as a coffee plantation would generally not constitute EUDR deforestation, because the passages do not indicate conversion of forest to agricultural use. However, canopy-loss data alone cannot establish this: loss may result from pruning, storms, fire, or harvesting and does not show agricultural conversion [Note: Hansen Global Forest Change loss is not deforestation]. The passages leave open how to classify particular boundary areas or changes in land use.

answers.question: Does forest degradation after 31 December 2020 make coffee non-compliant, or does that rule apply only to wood?
answers.answer:
Forest degradation after 31 December 2020 is a specific additional criterion for products containing or made using wood, not coffee. Article 2(13)(a) requires all relevant commodities, including coffee, to come from land not subject to deforestation after that date. Article 2(13)(b) separately addresses products containing or made using wood and requires that the wood be harvested without inducing forest degradation after that date [EUDR Art. 2(13)].

Thus, post-2020 forest degradation does not, on the wording provided, independently make coffee non-compliant. Coffee must still satisfy the deforestation-free criterion. The Commission’s guidance likewise describes the forest-degradation requirement as applying specifically to wood harvesting [EC FAQ Q4.5 (part 1)]. The passages do not address whether degradation might also constitute deforestation under other facts.

answers.question: If a forest is damaged by fire or a storm and then regrows, is that deforestation?
answers.answer:
No. Fire or storm damage alone is not “deforestation.” Under the EUDR, deforestation means converting forest to agricultural use, whether human-induced or not [EUDR Art. 2(3)]. Thus, a fire followed by conversion to agricultural land would be deforestation, but the fire itself would not be the reason [EC FAQ Q4.12].

If the affected forest is allowed to regenerate, it would not be deemed deforestation, and wood could be sourced once it has regrown [EC FAQ Q4.12]. Natural-event-related structural changes, including fire or storm damage, may also leave harvested products deforestation-free where harvesting did not induce the degradation, provided sufficient evidence supports that conclusion [EC FAQ Q4.7]. Restoration planting or seeding after fire or storms may likewise remain within the relevant forest categories where the stated conditions are met [EC FAQ Q4.9].

answers.question: How can the geolocation of a plot be checked against satellite images or forest cover maps?
answers.answer: Check the plot’s geolocation—latitude and longitude coordinates with at least six decimal digits; plots over four hectares generally require a polygon describing the perimeter [EUDR Art. 2(28)]. The operator should collect coordinates for every plot contributing to the product; if it cannot, the product should not be placed on the EU market or exported [EC FAQ Q1.19]. Those coordinates may then be cross-checked against satellite images or forest-cover maps to assess whether the product is deforestation-free [EC FAQ Q1.19]. Authorities may use Earth-observation data, including Copernicus tools, and other public or private technical sources [EUDR Art. 18(2)]. Maps are risk-assessment tools, not conclusive proof: being inside or outside a mapped forest area does not automatically establish non-compliance or compliance, given map coverage, accuracy, granularity, and other risk factors [EC FAQ Q9.10 (part 2)].

answers.question: What counts as a plot of land when a coffee estate has several parts?
answers.answer: A “plot of land” is land within a single real-estate property recognised under the production country’s law, with sufficiently homogeneous conditions to assess the aggregate deforestation and forest-degradation risk [EUDR Art. 2(27)]. Thus, a coffee estate may count as one plot if the entire property is sufficiently homogeneous; otherwise, only a distinct part may constitute the plot [EC FAQ Q1.15 (part 1)]. You need not include other plots owned by the same estate owner if they are not used to produce coffee covered by the Regulation or are not intended for the EU market [EC FAQ Q4.2]. If coffee comes from several separate plots, provide a separate polygon for each plot in the same due-diligence statement; one polygon cannot cover a wider estate containing multiple plots [EC FAQ Q1.14]. The passages leave the precise assessment of “sufficiently homogeneous” conditions to the facts and the production country’s property-law recognition.

answers.question: What does the EUDR require when a coffee plot is located in a designated reserve forest or protected area?
answers.answer: The EUDR does not make the reserve-forest or protected-area designation alone determinative on the supplied passage. It requires assessing the “legal status of the area of production,” which may mean the whole property rather than only the coffee plot under Article 2(40). If illegality elsewhere affects that legal status, coffee from the plot is not legal and therefore not compliant [EC FAQ Q1.15 (part 2)]. Any deforestation or forest degradation on declared plots automatically disqualifies commodities from those plots from being placed on the market or exported under Article 9(1)(d) [EC FAQ Q1.15 (part 2)]. The passage does not specify the separate legal consequences of a protected-area or reserve-forest designation, so those consequences remain open.

answers.question: Is clearing land or forming a plantation allowed inside a reserved forest in Karnataka?
answers.answer: Generally, no. In land covered by a Section 4 notification, the Karnataka Forest Act prohibits forming a plantation and making fresh clearings “for cultivation or for any other purpose.” [Karnataka Forest Act s.6] It also prohibits clearing or breaking up land for cultivation or any other purpose in a reserved forest, unless contrary rules or permission apply [Karnataka Forest Act s.24 (part 1)]. Section 6 preserves an exception for acts done under the written permission of the Forest Settlement Officer [Karnataka Forest Act s.6]. Unauthorised occupation of reserved-forest land may lead to summary eviction, and crops or trees raised there may be forfeited after an opportunity to be heard [Karnataka Forest Act s.64A (part 1)]. Thus, clearing or establishing a plantation is not allowed without the applicable written permission or other legally recognised exception; the passages do not specify every possible permission procedure or exception.

answers.question: Is rubber grown under trees treated as agricultural use or as forest?
answers.answer: Rubber grown under trees is treated as agricultural use, not forest, where it qualifies as an agricultural plantation or agroforestry system. The EUDR defines agricultural plantations to include “agroforestry systems where crops are grown under tree cover” and excludes them from “forest”; it also covers all plantations of relevant commodities other than wood [EUDR Art. 2(6)]. Commission guidance specifically confirms that rubber cultivation falls within this definition, including areas with rubber trees [EC FAQ Q4.14][EC Guidance §11.4(c)]. The legal classification therefore depends on the land meeting those agricultural-plantation criteria; the passages do not resolve every possible mixed or borderline land-use situation. Replacing a forest with a rubber plantation may nevertheless constitute deforestation under the Regulation [EC FAQ Q4.14].

answers.question: How can farmers give the location of their plots when land titles or property registers are missing?
answers.answer: Farmers can collect and provide the geolocation of the plots they use even if those plots are not recorded in a land registry and they lack identification documents or titles [EC FAQ Q1.10 (part 1)]. The geolocation must give latitude and longitude coordinates with at least six decimal digits; for plots over four hectares used for relevant commodities other than cattle, it must use a polygon with enough points to describe the perimeter [EUDR Art. 2(28)]. The absence of a registry or formal title should not prevent land that is de facto used as a plot from being designated [EC FAQ Q1.6]. The Regulation does not require a title where domestic law does not require one to produce and commercialise agricultural products, but operators must still verify compliance with applicable national laws [EC FAQ Q1.10 (part 1)].

answers.question: What is the difference between forest and other wooded land in the regulation?
answers.answer:
Under the regulation, “forest” is land spanning more than 0.5 hectares with trees higher than 5 metres and canopy cover “of more than 10 %”, or trees “able to reach those thresholds in situ”, excluding land predominantly under agricultural or urban land use [EUDR Art. 2(4)].

“Other wooded land” is land “not classified as ‘forest’”, also spanning more than 0.5 hectares, with trees higher than 5 metres and canopy cover “of 5 to 10 %”, or trees able to reach those thresholds in situ; alternatively, it may have combined shrub, bush and tree cover above 10 %. It also excludes land predominantly under agricultural or urban land use [EUDR Art. 2(12)].

The passages leave open how borderline cases are classified beyond these stated thresholds.

answers.question: What fines and other penalties can be imposed for breaking the regulation?
answers.answer:
Member States must establish penalties for infringements by operators, downstream operators and traders [EUDR Art. 25(1)]. Penalties must be “effective, proportionate and dissuasive.” [EUDR Art. 25(2)] They include:

- Fines proportionate to environmental damage and the value of the commodities/products, designed to remove economic benefits; repeated infringements attract increasing fines. For legal persons, the maximum must be at least 4% of the preceding financial year’s total Union-wide turnover, increased where necessary to exceed the benefit gained [EUDR Art. 25(2)].
- Confiscation of the relevant products [EUDR Art. 25(2)].
- Confiscation of revenues from transactions involving them [EUDR Art. 25(2)].
- Temporary exclusion, for up to 12 months, from public procurement and public funding [EUDR Art. 25(2)].
- Temporary prohibition on placing or making products available on the market or exporting them for serious or repeated infringements [EUDR Art. 25(2)].
- Prohibition on using simplified due diligence for serious or repeated infringements [EUDR Art. 25(2)].

National rules determine implementation [EUDR Art. 25(1)].

answers.question: Who can declare land to be a reserved forest in Karnataka?
answers.answer: In Karnataka, the State Government can constitute land as a reserved forest, provided the land is Government property, subject to Government proprietary rights, or concerns forest produce to which the Government is entitled [Karnataka Forest Act s.3]. It must first issue a notification declaring the decision, describing the land’s situation and limits, and appointing a Forest Settlement Officer to inquire into claimed rights [Karnataka Forest Act s.4]. After the statutory claims, appeals, and other proceedings are completed, the State Government must publish a further notification clearly specifying the forest’s limits and declaring it a reserved forest from the stated date [Karnataka Forest Act s.17]. Thus, the Forest Settlement Officer conducts the settlement inquiry; the State Government makes the declaration.

answers.question: Is forest cleared to build a road after 2020 counted as deforestation?
answers.answer: Not necessarily. The EUDR rule defines “deforestation-free” by whether the relevant commodity was produced on land “not … subject to deforestation after 31 December 2020.” [EUDR Art. 2(13)] The passages specify that deforestation encompasses conversion of forest to agricultural use, including after the cut-off date [EC FAQ Q4.12]. They do not state that clearing forest to build a road is itself deforestation, nor do they define road construction as agricultural use. Therefore, the passages leave open whether road-building clearance falls within “deforestation”; the fact that it occurred after 2020 alone does not resolve that question. The cut-off date is 31 December 2020 [EUDR Art. 2(13)].

A plot of land is land within a single real-estate property recognised under the production country’s law, with sufficiently homogeneous conditions for assessing deforestation and forest-degradation risk [EUDR Art. 2(27)]. The guidance therefore leaves open how the production country’s law recognises such communal or public land and how its boundaries and homogeneous conditions are established.
